title: Generics & launch 0: Orientation
disclaimer: An educational course for project management of generic launches. It is not regulatory, legal or quality advice: EU rules are the anchor, and national and company practice vary.

lessons.title: The generic business in one page

blocks.markdown:
## What a generic is

A **generic medicine** (*médicament générique*) contains the same active substance as a medicine that's already authorised. It's taken in the same way and works the same way in the body. That earlier medicine is the **reference product** (*médicament de référence*). Its own trial data protect it for a set period. Once that protection runs out, generics can be authorised by relying on the reference product's data, instead of repeating its clinical trials.

The moment protection ends is called **loss of exclusivity** (*perte d'exclusivité*). Module 1 explains the exact rules.

blocks.alt: Line chart: originator price stays near 100, then drifts down after loss of exclusivity; generic price enters about 25% lower and is about 40% lower after two years
blocks.caption: What happens to price after loss of exclusivity

blocks.markdown:
## Why price, volume and speed decide everything

When the European Commission studied medicines that faced generic competition between 2000 and 2007, it found two things. Generics entered at prices about 25% below the originator's price before loss of exclusivity. After two years, they were on average about 40% below.

So each pack earns little. A generic business makes money through **volume** (many packs) and **speed** (being on the market early, before prices fall further and before many competitors arrive). The Commission also noted that every week of delay in generic entry has a cost.

## Not every launch is a pure generic

Some of your launches won't be classic generics. A product that combines two known active substances in one tablet uses **Art. 10b**, the fixed-combination route. A product filed with a complete dossier of its own uses **Art. 8(3)**, the full or stand-alone route. Module 1 covers both. In every case, the business logic of this lesson still applies.
**What this means for the launch timeline:** in generics, time is money. Every avoidable week between approval and first sale is lost volume, which is why the PM role matters.

cards.back: Same active substance, same way of taking it, same effect in the body as an authorised reference product. FR: médicament générique.
The moment the reference product's protection ends and generics can enter. FR: perte d'exclusivité.

questions.stem: According to the European Commission's sector inquiry, how much cheaper were generics on average two years after entry?
questions.explanation: About 25% below the originator's earlier price at entry, and about 40% below after two years (averages for 2000–2007).

## The cast

A generic launch involves several companies and several named people. One company can play more than one role. This map shows the main ones.

blocks.alt: Diagram: dossier owner to manufacturer to EU importer and QP to distributor to pharmacy; MAH linked by dashed lines to manufacturer, importer, regulatory affairs and QPPV
blocks.caption: Who's who in a generic launch

blocks.markdown:
## Who owns the data

The **dossier owner** (*détenteur du dossier*) is the company that developed the product and owns the data behind it, often the manufacturer. When it lets another company use that dossier, it acts as the **licensor** (*concédant de licence*).

## Who is legally responsible

The **MAH** (*titulaire de l'autorisation de mise sur le marché*) holds the marketing authorisation and answers to the authorities for the product. EU law requires the MAH to be established in the EU or EEA. That's why a manufacturer based in India usually works through an EU company that holds the licence.

## Who makes it and who lets it into the EU

The **manufacturer** makes the product. A product made outside the EU must come in through an EU site that holds an **MIA** (*autorisation de fabrication et d'importation*), a manufacturing and importation authorisation. At that site, a **QP** (*personne qualifiée*), or Qualified Person, certifies every batch before it can be sold. Module 6 explains why this is a key step for products from India.

## Who handles regulatory work and safety

**Regulatory affairs** (*affaires réglementaires*) prepares submissions, answers questions from the authorities and manages later changes. The **QPPV** (*responsable de la pharmacovigilance*) is the named person responsible for monitoring the product's safety once it's on the market. EU law requires the QPPV to live and work in the EU.

## Who gets it to patients

A **wholesaler** (*grossiste-répartiteur*) needs a wholesale distribution authorisation and must follow good distribution practice. Wholesalers move the product to pharmacies and hospitals. A local partner or affiliate often handles sales and tenders.

## Contracts decide who does what

The companies in a launch are tied together by a set of written agreements. A PM rarely negotiates them, but reads them often, because the answer to 'who is doing this?' is usually in one of them.

blocks.alt: Diagram: MAH at the centre, linked to the dossier owner (licence and supply), manufacturer and importer (quality agreement), PV provider (PV agreement) and distributor (distribution)
blocks.caption: The agreements that bind a launch

blocks.markdown:
## Licence and supply agreement

The **licence and supply agreement** (*contrat de licence et d'approvisionnement*) gives the MAH the right to use the dossier in certain countries, and sets how the product will be supplied. It typically covers:

- territory and exclusivity
- prices and payments
- forecasts and minimum orders
- lead times
- who pays for regulatory work

This is standard industry practice; contract structures and names vary.

## Quality agreement

Whenever a GMP activity is outsourced, EU GMP requires a written contract that defines each party's responsibilities. That contract is the **quality agreement** (*contrat qualité*). It sets out who tests, who releases, who handles complaints and deviations, and who approves changes.

### Process card: Quality agreement

- What it is: the written GMP contract between the MAH or importer and the manufacturer
- Who owns it: the Quality teams on both sides; the QP must agree with it
- Inputs: the supply agreement, the site's GMP status, the testing and release plan
- Output: a signed agreement with a responsibility table
- Typical duration: weeks, longer if the sites disagree on responsibilities
- What makes it slip: unclear testing split, missing site audit, legal back-and-forth
- PM watch-points: it must be signed before commercial supply and QP release; track it as a launch milestone

## PV agreement and distribution agreement

A **PV agreement** (*accord de pharmacovigilance*), often called an SDEA (safety data exchange agreement), sets how safety information moves between partners, and within what deadlines. A distribution agreement covers the wholesaler or local partner. Both are standard practice, and their names vary.
**What this means for the launch timeline:** missing or unsigned agreements are a classic hidden blocker. Put each one on the plan with an owner and a target date.

cards.back: A written GMP contract defining each party's responsibilities for outsourced activities, required by EU GMP Chapter 7. FR: contrat qualité.
Gives rights to use a dossier in a territory, and sets how the product is supplied (prices, forecasts, lead times). FR: contrat de licence et d'approvisionnement.

questions.stem: Which agreement does EU GMP explicitly require when manufacturing or testing is outsourced?
questions.explanation: EudraLex Vol. 4, Chapter 7 requires a written contract covering the responsibilities for outsourced activities, known as the quality agreement.

## Two routes to the same shelf

A company can get a generic onto the market in two ways: develop it itself, or take an existing dossier from someone who already developed it. Much of your work will involve the second route.

blocks.alt: Diagram comparing two routes: in-licensing goes deal, dossier transfer, submission, approval, launch; own development adds formulation, bioequivalence study and dossier writing before submission
blocks.caption: Two routes to a launch

blocks.markdown:
## In-licensing

With **in-licensing** (*acquisition de licence*), the company acquires the right to use another company's finished dossier. It skips product development, so the route is usually faster. The trade-off is dependence: on the quality of someone else's data, and on their supply.

## Own development

With own development, the company formulates the product, runs the bioequivalence study and writes the dossier itself. This gives more control, but takes longer and needs investment upfront.

## The other side of the deal

The same deal seen from the dossier owner's side is **out-licensing** (*concession de licence*): granting rights to its dossier to partners in other countries. In business development you see both directions, sometimes for the same product in different markets.

attributes.label: Dependence or control
values: Depends on the partner's data and supply
Full control of data and process

attributes.label: What it takes
values: Starts with dossier transfer and gap analysis

blocks.markdown: **What this means for the launch timeline:** for in-licensed products, the plan starts at the deal: dossier transfer and gap analysis are the first critical steps.

cards.back: Acquiring the right to use another company's dossier. Faster than own development, but dependent on the partner. FR: acquisition de licence.
Granting a partner the right to use your dossier in its territory. FR: concession de licence.

It doesn't need a marketing authorisation

## Five things to keep in hand

1. Scope: which products, strengths, packs and countries
2. Timeline
3. Owners
4. Risks
5. Decisions

Everything else in this course feeds one of these five.

blocks.markdown:
## Timeline tools

A **Gantt chart** (*diagramme de Gantt*) shows tasks as bars over time, with dependencies and milestones. The **critical path** (*chemin critique*) is the chain of tasks with no slack: if any one of them slips, the launch date slips. Milestones such as 'submission', 'approval' and 'first batch released' are the dates management asks about.

## Ownership and risk tools

A **RACI** (*matrice RACI*) lists, for each task, who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed. A **risk register** (*registre des risques*) lists what could go wrong, how likely it is, its impact, and the mitigation. A decision log records what was decided, by whom and when.

## A simple weekly rhythm

A short weekly status update works well: what moved, what's late, the top three risks and the decisions needed, with a red, amber or green flag per country. These are practical PM conventions, not regulatory rules.
**What this means for the launch timeline:** the PM's job is to make the critical path visible early, and to keep it honest every week.

cards.back: The chain of tasks with no slack: if one slips, the launch slips. FR: chemin critique.
For each task: who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed. FR: matrice RACI.

questions.stem: A task on the critical path slips by two weeks, with nothing else changing. What happens to the launch date?
options: It slips by about two weeks
questions.explanation: By definition, critical-path tasks have no slack, so a delay passes straight to the end date.

blocks.markdown:
## One fixed anchor

In the **decentralised procedure** (*procédure décentralisée*), the lead country has 120 days to draft its assessment, and the other countries then have 90 days to approve it. That makes about 210 days of assessment, plus pauses while the company answers questions (clock-stops). Module 2 walks through the clock.

Most other steps don't have a legal deadline. They depend on people, contracts and supply, and that's where planning makes the biggest difference.

## How the modules map to the timeline

- **Module 1:** what kind of product it is
- **Module 2:** how it gets approved
- **Module 3:** when it may legally launch
- **Modules 4–6:** how it's made, tested and imported
- **Modules 7–8:** what's in the pack and on it
- **Module 9:** the whole timeline together

cards.back: A procedure in which one country leads the assessment and the others approve it. About 210 days of assessment plus clock-stops. FR: procédure décentralisée.

cards.front: Which steps have a legal clock?
cards.back: Mainly the decentralised procedure assessment (about 210 days plus clock-stops). Most other steps depend on people, contracts and supply.

questions.explanation: Directive 2001/83/EC sets 120 days for the lead country's draft assessment and 90 days for the other countries to approve. Most other steps depend on planning.
